messages.subject: Re: Population prevalence
parts:
I'd say that it isn't a "downside" per se, but it is a bit pointless/futile. As the whole point of providing a population prevalence is to facilitate liability scale conversion, because clinically ascertained samples tend to have an inflated number of cases, which creates an upward bias in heritability estimates (and any downstream metrics which would incorporate heritability into its calculation). So if you don't have a population prevalence, setting it to equal the sample prevalence is just going to get you your estimates on the observed rather than the liability scale. And the extent of this biasing will be exacerbated, the bigger the discrepancy between the sample prevalence and the population prevalence (i.e. a sample prev of 40% and a pop prev of 30% will be less of a biased inflation than 40% sample prev, 0.1% pop prev). Out of curiosity, what is the phenotype?

On Thu, 24 Jun 2021 at 18:46, Lucy <whatawo...@gmail.com> wrote:
Are there any downsides to setting the population prevalence as the sample prevalence if you cannot find other studies that state the population prevalence for your trait?
